hypothesis: The coefficient of variation (CV = SD / mean) of human stature and of weight at a given age tracks the mean rate of growth at that age: it falls through childhood as growth decelerates, rises again during the adolescent growth spurt, and falls after it. Hence, across ages, CV should be positively associated with growth velocity, within childhood as well as over the whole span, and the CV peak should coincide with the velocity peak.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using the CDC 2000 growth-chart LMS reference tables for stature-for-age and weight-for-age (2-20 years, half-month grid, each sex), compute at each age the CV of the fitted Box-Cox distribution (mean and SD obtained by numerical integration over z in [-4, 4]; the LMS S parameter is reported as a check) and the growth velocity dM/dt (central differences of the median M, per year). For each of the four series (stature boys, stature girls, weight boys, weight girls), over ages 2.5-19.5 years: (T1) Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive with P < 0.01; (T2) the age of maximum CV between 8 and 19 years lies within 1.5 years of the age of peak velocity (the adolescent spurt), and CV at that peak exceeds the pre-pubertal minimum CV (ages 4-11) by at least 5% of its value; (T3) within childhood, from 2.5 years to the age of minimum velocity before the spurt, Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive (CV falls as growth decelerates). The claim is supported if T1, T2 and T3 all hold in at least 3 of the 4 series.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered (claim refuted). T1 fails (rho <= 0, or P >= 0.01) in at least 3 of the 4 series, or T3 shows a significant negative rho (CV rising while growth decelerates, P < 0.01) in at least 3 of the 4 series. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. the adolescent rise T2 holds everywhere but the childhood decline T3 does not). If the CDC tables cannot be retrieved the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).
interpretation: Thompson's evidence was Bowditch's and Boas & Wissler's cross-sectional CVs of Boston schoolchildren, ages 5-18 (stature CV about 4.8% at 5, 4.4% at 9, 5.8% at 14, 3.7% at 18). Modern reference charts are smoothed cross-sectional distributions of the same kind, so the LMS S parameter (approximately the CV) by age is the direct analogue. 'Rate of growth' is read as the absolute velocity of the median (cm/yr, kg/yr), Thompson's own usage (his Fig. 4 is the curve of annual increments). The WHO 2007 reference (5-19 years, height-for-age, both sexes) is a secondary replication, and the CDC infant tables (length and weight for age, 0-36 months) a descriptive check of Pearson's statement that variability decreases from birth; neither enters the verdict. Known confound (assessors): the adolescent CV rise is produced largely by variation in the timing of the spurt rather than by the rate itself; this does not affect the empirical association tested here. Before this pre-registration a reachability probe fetched statage.csv and wtage.csv and printed their header and first two rows (age 24 and 24.5 months); nothing else was inspected.
